narrative: Your application for university admission was unfortunately rejected because our model predicts a 51% probability that you would not pass the bar exam on your first attempt. While this prediction is only slightly above the threshold for concern, it suggests that based on historical data, your current academic profile presents a higher risk than the university typically accepts. To help you understand this decision, we looked at ten "what if" scenarios—alternative versions of your application that would have resulted in an approval. Interestingly, your undergraduate GPA of 3.70 is actually significantly higher than the 3.24 average of students who successfully pass the bar, which shows you have strong academic potential. However, the model is placing heavy emphasis on your performance during law school and your standardized testing. Your law school grades in your first and third years placed you in the 3rd and 1st deciles respectively, which is quite a bit lower than the 6th decile average seen in successful candidates. Despite these challenges and your status as a part-time student from a lower-middle-income background, the model indicates that your path to success is very specific. In every single one of the ten alternative scenarios we analyzed, the only factor that needed to change to flip your prediction to a "pass" was your LSAT score. While your current LSAT score is 34, the model consistently found that increasing this score by just two points to a 36 would be enough to change the outcome. It is notable that other factors, such as your family income or your decision to study part-time, did not need to change in any of the scenarios to achieve a positive result. This means the model doesn't see your personal circumstances as insurmountable barriers, but rather views the LSAT as a critical indicator of your bar exam readiness. Because the LSAT was the only feature that changed in 100% of our simulations, it is the most actionable lever you have to improve your standing. On average, a modest improvement of two points on the LSAT would bring you much closer to the 37.27 average of students who pass the bar. If you are able to retake the exam and achieve that 36, the model's prediction would shift from a failure to a predicted pass. We encourage you to focus your efforts on this specific metric, as it appears to be the primary bridge between your current rejection and a future admission.
